Building a mathematical drawing machine (often called a Spirograph or Harmonograph) is a fantastic way to blend your interests in geometry and robotics. Since you have the NXT system, you can move beyond simple gears and use software to control the complexity of the patterns.

Here are three distinct ways you could approach the build:

1. The XY-Plotter (Cartesian Style)

This is the most "software engineer" approach. It functions like a CNC machine or a 3D printer.

  • The Mechanism: One motor moves a carriage along the X-axis, while a second motor moves the paper or a second rail along the Y-axis. A third motor (or a simple lever) lifts the pen up and down.
  • The Math: You can program the NXT to plot functions like $y = \sin(x)$ or create Lissajous curves.
  • The Challenge: Managing the "backlash" or physical play in the LEGO gears to ensure the lines meet up perfectly.

2. The Rotary Harmonograph (Lissajous Machine)

This version uses two rotating platforms to create "nested" circular motion.

  • The Mechanism: Motor A rotates a large circular platform where the paper sits. Motor B controls a long arm holding the pen that swings across the paper.
  • The Math: By varying the speed ratio between the two motors (e.g., 2:3 or 1:1.5), you create different "lobed" patterns.
  • The Challenge: Use the NXT's Rotation Sensors (built into the motors) to ensure the speeds stay constant even as the battery voltage drops.

3. The Pantograph (Mechanical Linkage)

This is a more "analog" feel, similar to your interest in wooden automatons.

  • The Mechanism: Use long LEGO Technic beams to create a parallelogram linkage. One "anchor" point is fixed, one point is moved by motors, and the third point holds the pen.
  • The Math: This build explores scaling and transformation. A small movement by the motors is amplified into a large movement by the pen.
  • The Challenge: Calculating the joint angles required to move the pen to a specific $(x, y)$ coordinate—this is a classic robotics problem known as Inverse Kinematics.

Suggested "NXT-Level" Features

To make this project unique to your background, consider adding these layers:

  • Musical Input: Use the NXT Sound Sensor. Program the machine to increase the "amplitude" of its drawing (the motor power or travel distance) whenever it detects a loud clap or a specific beat from a song.
  • Interactive Controls: Use the NXT buttons or a touch sensor to "live-adjust" the variables of the math equation while the machine is drawing.
  • Data Logging: Have the NXT log the coordinates it "drew" to a text file on the brick, which you can later import into SketchUp to see a 3D digital version of your 2D physical drawing.

The Pantograph (Option 3) is a fascinating project because it relies on Euclidean geometry and mechanical linkages rather than just raw motor power. It is essentially a physical analog computer for scaling drawings.

The Core Geometry: The Parallelogram

The machine is built using four Technic beams connected at pivot points to form a parallelogram.

  1. The Fixed Pivot (Point A): This point is anchored to the NXT base or a heavy surface. It never moves.
  2. The Input (Point B): This is where your NXT motors are attached. As the motors move this joint, they change the angles of the parallelogram.
  3. The Output (Point C): This is where the pen is held.

Because the beams are connected in a parallel structure, the movement of the pen (Point C) will always be a perfectly scaled-up version of the movement at the input (Point B).

How to Motorize it with NXT

In a traditional hand-drawn pantograph, you trace a shape at Point B. In your robotic version, the motors create the shape:

  • Dual-Motor Drive: You can use two NXT motors to control the "elbow" and "shoulder" of the linkage.
  • The Math (Forward Kinematics): If Motor 1 turns $\theta_1$ degrees and Motor 2 turns $\theta_2$ degrees, you can use trigonometry to calculate exactly where the pen is: $$x = L_1 \cos(\theta_1) + L_2 \cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$$ $$y = L_1 \sin(\theta_1) + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$$
  • Scaling: By changing where you "pin" the beams together (moving the joints to different holes in the Technic beams), you change the scaling ratio. This allows you to draw very large, sweeping curves from very small, precise motor movements.

Why this fits your skills

  • Mathematics: It’s a physical manifestation of similar triangles. If the ratio of the beam lengths is $1:3$, every tiny movement of the motor results in a drawing three times as large.
  • Software Engineering: To draw a square or a circle, you have to solve Inverse Kinematics. You decide where you want the pen to go $(x, y)$, and your code must calculate the exact motor degrees $(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ needed to get there.

Prototyping Tip

Since you have a lot of NXT parts, I recommend building the linkage with long Technic 15-M beams. Use the "frictionless" pins (the light gray or tan ones) for the pivots so the machine moves smoothly without "stuttering."
